title: The Classical Boundary of Quantum Computation: History-Resolved Causal Stochastic Machines and the Cost of Classicalization
authors: Kyoungho Cho, Junghee Ryu, Minsu Kim, Jeongho Bang
abstract: What separates quantum computation from classical computation when a classical model may retain every branch history and arbitrary causal memory? We study this question using history-resolved causal stochastic machines (HCSMs), which describe positive causal history laws. Probabilistic Turing machines (PTMs) embed in stochastic-ensemble models (SEnMs), which in turn embed in HCSMs. We prove that HCSM history laws coincide exactly with the fixed-basis, prefix-preserving diagonal sector of ideal quantum processes, denoted by $\mathsf{PTM}_{\rm proc}$ and distinguished here from algorithmic quantum Turing machines (QTMs). Coherent quantum processes extend strictly beyond this sector. The boundary is already visible in reversibility. Born-probability shadows of unitary gates preserve inverse composition exactly for basis permutations with phases. Outside this class, an exact positive stochastic simulation that supports universal quantum continuations must retain predictive information absent from visible probabilities. An inverse-recovery identity quantifies this phase ledger, and universal continuation forces the retained probability law to be tomographically sufficient for the quantum state. Under continuous full-state encoding assumptions, this requirement yields quantum-state dimension lower bounds. The familiar slogan $\mathsf{PTM}\subseteq\mathsf{QTM}$ is thereby sharpened into a precise classical boundary and a no-free-classicalization principle. Complete classical branching does not remove the predictive information needed to represent quantum coherence.
summary: This work rigorously defines the classical boundary of quantum computation by comparing History-Resolved Causal Stochastic Machines (HCSMs) to quantum processes. It proves that classical simulation, even with full history memory, is restricted to a specific, diagonal sector of quantum dynamics. This establishes a precise 'no-free-classicalization principle,' showing that retaining full classical history cannot simulate all quantum phenomena.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental structural boundary separating quantum computation from classical computation, even when the classical model retains full causal history and memory.
main_result: The authors prove that the history laws of the strong classical model (HCSMs) coincide exactly with a specific, diagonal sector of ideal quantum processes, establishing a precise 'no-free-classicalization principle.'
method: The study uses formal embedding theorems to map Probabilistic Turing Machines into History-Resolved Causal Stochastic Machines, comparing their predictive power against full quantum process descriptions.
model_or_system: The primary model is the History-Resolved Causal Stochastic Machine (HCSM), a strong classical model retaining full causal history. This is compared against ideal quantum processes ($	ext{QTM}_{	ext{proc}}$) and standard Probabilistic Turing Machines (PTMs).
key_observables: Phase Ledger, Predictive Information, Acceptance Probability, and the comparison between HCSM history laws and quantum process compositionality.
important_parameters: The boundary itself, quantified by the required predictive information beyond visible probabilities, and the dimension bounds derived from continuous state encoding.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes continuous full-state encoding and focuses on compositional process simulation, which is a strong requirement.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates an HCSM as a causal stochastic tree over full histories, showing how probabilities are calculated via history-dependent kernels.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first defining the HCSM as a rigorous classical model, then proving its embedding into quantum processes, and finally using information-theoretic tools (like the ledger cost) to quantify the necessary information that distinguishes quantum coherence from classical stochasticity.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, information-theoretic characterization of what makes quantum computation fundamentally non-classical, which is crucial for understanding resource theories in quantum information.
